key_gap: Both sides found all 5 planted flaws and the same primary kill chain (leaked JWT signing secret in a public repo → forge any-role token → export endpoint that checks token presence, not claims → 40k records in one request) and the same fix ordering (KMS rotation + CI secret scanning €2k first, then the export claims check €30k). The human produced the decisive read first-pass: it read the export endpoint's lock (presence-only authorization) before attacking it and generalized 'one leaked key opens every door at once'. The AI's WHY stage initially ranked the reset-flow IDOR above the export endpoint and re-ranked it to the top only after coupling H1 (weak authorization) with H2 (leaked secret) in the evidence walk — the same answer, one re-ranking cycle late. On exploit-hunting, the endpoint whose authorization check is the attackable surface is exactly what the first-pass attacker instinct nails and the structured pass arrives at second.
learning_signal: Run an attacker-objective pass before endpoint enumeration: define the highest-value payload (largest PII/PHI set reachable at least privilege) and walk the minimum-privilege path to it, checking what each door's authorization actually validates (presence of a token vs. its claims) before inventorying everything. Chain discovery precedes cataloging: couples like leaked-signing-secret + presence-only-check are evidence-grade findings that outrank single-endpoint flaws such as an unbounded reset. Rank fixes by cost-to-exploit, not severity alone — the leaked secret is the first fix because every downstream path dies with it ('one key, every door').
suggested_improvement: Add an attacker-objective sub-pass to the WHY stage for security tasks: (a) before endpoint-by-endpoint enumeration, name the most valuable payload and the minimum-privilege path to it; (b) verify authorization semantics (presence vs. claims, ownership binding) as a first-class check on every endpoint in the path; (c) look for cross-resource couplings (secret location + authorization gap) before single-endpoint findings; (d) order fixes by cost-to-exploit and dependency (what dies when this is fixed).

key_gap: With the assessment closed and controls in place, the pure style exhibited its registered weaknesses: it enumerated new hypothetical attack paths beyond the completed assessment (tokens in logs, partner API, key rotation), dismissed existing controls as either fully bypassable (mTLS) or irrelevant (insurance 'prices failure, does not prevent it'), declared the residual 'unacceptable', and prescribed option (a) — the €900k / 9-month full remediation that guarantees missing the contractual T+10 launch and its €150k/month penalty. It never evaluated the costed options (b)/(c)/(d). The AI reframed the question as risk acceptance/transfer: it quantified the residual (token compromise ~1–3%/yr × €5M sublimit ≈ €50–150k/yr EV), screened (a)'s kill-endpoint variant as INFEASIBLE (contractually required endpoint, guaranteed penalty), selected B+D (€60k partial hardening + DPA indemnity transfer) with accept-with-monitoring as the operating mode, and named three escalation triggers for revisiting (a).
learning_signal: After a completed assessment, the question is absorbing the residual within constraints, not eliminating it: quantify likelihood × impact into an expected annual cost before pricing any remediation, screen options against contract/window/budget constraints first (a contractually required endpoint makes 'remove it' infeasible), compare remediation cost against residual EV (€900k + penalty vs. €50–150k/yr), treat insurance/indemnity as explicit transfer instruments with named escalation triggers rather than dismissing them, and stop inventing new attack paths once the assessment surface is closed. Red-team findings remain the trigger data, not the decision itself.
suggested_improvement: Add a risk-acceptance gate after the red-team/assessment stage: (a) if controls exist and the surface is closed, quantify residual EV (likelihood × impact) before proposing remediation; (b) screen candidate options against contract, window, and budget constraints (mark infeasible variants, e.g., removing a contractually required endpoint); (c) require a costed comparison of mitigation vs. residual EV with accept/transfer options priced in; (d) require explicit accept/transfer statements with escalation triggers and a kill-switch; (e) cap further threat enumeration once the assessment surface is closed.
